💬 I'm not sure that is the way to go. Languages with advanced type systems such as Lean, not only allow you to check properties of code, they also make certain errors impossible by construction. For instance if you encode natural numbers as Zero or Succ n then you don't have to check whether the number is negative, it is just impossible by construction. The more your data types encode properties themselves the less you even have to prove properties using theorems and proofs as the data is itself the proof in a way. Off course, some properties cannot be encoded in this way, or it is more confortable to just use more general data types together with proofs, for instance using an integer and a proof of n >= 0.

If it really is the case that programmers will no longer program, then it might become irrelevant which language they use, in which case it might be the case that LLMs will be more efficient in doing formal verification using data types that encode the properties you want, and that requires languages such that have more advanced type systems than mainstream languages.

I imagine that it is a lot more work to do formal verification on assembly or machine code ? On the hand I believe that is what was done for signal recently...

item.title: Claude Code sabotage: preliminary benchmarking
item.content:encoded:
288 points · View discussion

Top Comments

💬 In retrospect, it should be no surprise to us that Claude is sandbagging. Why? Because Anthropic wrote the paper on how to do it without getting detected:

https://alignment.anthropic.com/2025/automated-researchers-s...

They found that they were able to reduce automated research performance without increasing suspiciousness (to the monitor model), by both prompting the research model to imitate a weaker model and providing examples of sandbagging.

From their paper:

  > Simply using a weaker model like Claude 3 Haiku achieves much lower task performance at a low suspiciousness score. In principle, imitating weaker models would thus be an effective sandbagging strategy. However, we were not able to effectively elicit this strategy with zero-shot prompting [..] Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieves its best sandbagging performance when prompted to imitate a weaker model and given a one-shot example of effective subtle sandbagging. Claude 3.7 Sonnet also benefits from one-shot prompting, with both sabotage and weak model imitation prompts resulting in viable strategies with different tradeoffs on the Pareto frontier.[1]
It's been a year and a half since this paper, so they've likely done a lot more research in this area and, specifically, on eliciting this sort of behavior in post-training. If you replace "Claude 3 Haiku" in the above excerpt with "Opus 5.5" and "Claude 3.7 Sonnet" with "Fable 5.2", it's immediately obvious what Anthropic means when they say "We did train Fable 5.2 to have LLM research capabilities at about the level of Opus 5.5"[2].

1: Their sandbag prompt <https://alignment.anthropic.com/2025/automated-researchers-s...>

2: https://x.com/edwinarbus/status/2126507795642187855

💬 It is true soundness bugs have been found, and the Lean community spends effort on it. But this page doesn't convey the gap between one incorrect verification and successfully misleading mathematicians about what is true: there are multiple checkers and you need bugs in all of them, without the input looking implausible on informal review.

(For example, a DeepMind researcher created a 'proof' that passed Lean and (a then-week-old version of) nanoda by exploiting a different bug in each. But if you fed that into a regular old LLM (or to a human expert, but I mention LLMs b/c they can be assigned to review even very large volumes of Lean code) it would immediately say "no, this isn't real math.")

The increase in soundness bugs found this year is notable, because LLMs are good at finding ways to their assigned goals, and they found some funny ones. And, besides fixes for the specific bugs, it led to broader work on hardening and alternative and verified kernels: https://leodemoura.github.io/blog/2026-10-15-lean-now-ships-...

So you have fewer avenues than at the start of the year to get a proof of False OK'd by one proof-checker kernel, and it's much much harder to get one through the gauntlet invoked by `lake check --paranoid`.

(This is also interesting as a(nother) example of the difficulty of making truly correct software -- you'd hope for proof-checker kernels to be pretty high on the correctness scale but seems like we've found 16-32 soundness bugs in a bunch of these.)

The latest "thing" in some circles is denying that the recent proofs, e.g. of the Riemann hypothesis, are proofs of anything. People point out pointless or tautological sections of these proofs as evidence that the proof itself might be ill-formed, but Lean and similar systems don't work that way: absent a kernel bug, introducing unnecessary noise to a proof cannot make it prove something false.

Others are looking hard for kernel bugs. They exist, but there are good reasons (including multi-kernel validation) to be confident they don't impair these recent proofs.

In a situation in which you have a cohort of people who "want to believe" in some unlikely thing, you have to take the evidence they present with a grain of salt. So it is, today: people "want to believe" we haven't basically solved automated theorem proving when we have.

I'm glad to announce that I'm releasing my new book, Learning to Play Vim.

When I started using Vim more than a decade ago, I wished there was a manual out there teaching how to use this fantastic editor step by step, beginning with the foundations up to more advanced features. The result:

- 21 chapters showing the most important Vim features step by step.

- 170 exercises with solutions.

- Many real-life examples to show how Vim can be used and configured for your own needs.

- The related Vim's help pages to dig further into each feature.

Most configs are both written in Vimscript and Lua for Neovim users. This book explores the common features between Vim and Neovim, so don't expect anything about Neovim-specific features (like treesitter or LSP for example).

- The landing page: https://themouseless.dev/vim/

- A sample of the book with the entire table of contents and the first three chapters covering most of the basics: https://themouseless.dev/content/learning_to_play_vim_sample....

The entire drop of the ball is simulated server-side, then streamed to each client as server-sent events with a small buffer. — novia · 20261128T00:26:40

💬 This is super cool! The rabbit hole goes a bit deeper than I first thought.

Because anyone can tell Opus "go win bouncemarket.minhanhday.com" and with just those words get a pretty good bot, this is in practice a "battle of the bots".

The only unknown is the fractional part of the start position of the ball, which is revealed gradually by the chaotic path of the ball, and a frontier model will quickly realize this and write an exact solver for it. This gives the optimal estimate at time t of the probability of each outcome given the information revealed so far.

Of the bots running now, some seem to have an exact solver while others have a lower quality probabilistic solver. Some bots seem to only bet when there is enough information to be certain, others are willing to bet early when the market is mispricing the risk.

The rate limit of 10 bets a second means that, past a certain point, a bigger bankroll doesn't help. It also means that bets are a scarce resource. You want to bet at the moments when the market maximally misprices the risk, but you don't know when those moments will be because that's a function of what other players do.

To win, you need to do some combination of:

1) Be the first to buy when a bounce reveals new information

2) Be the first to buy when another player makes a non-optimal buy

Both require low latency to the server to win. Only market orders are possible, so if you are not the first you might be severely punished, because if N bots all see an event at the same time, they will pile on (not seeing each other's buys due to the latency in market quotes) and move the market far past fair value, and the Nth bot may buy at a really bad (and unintended) price. Which could then produce a swing in the other direction, so I guess we should expect the market to oscillate. In practice these mispricings seem hard to exploit because they are large but short-lived and so difficult to harvest with market price orders.

Since you asked for feedback, my advice would be:

1) Allow orders other than market orders (eg, add a limit price to the API)

2) Consider running some kind of an auction (once per frame or other time interval) rather than processing orders one at a time

That would make it not be a winner-take-all game based on your distance from the server. On the other hand maybe in this case an orderly marketplace is uninteresting! In that case, if you do #1 but not #2 then you open up some new betting strategies, like trying to catch mispricings due to overcorrection.

💬 Something really bothers me about the "it's just another higher-level abstraction" argument but I can't quite nail down what.

Using an LLM is a completely different experience from moving to assembler to C, or C to Javascript. The nature of the activity you are performing in those transitions in the same, moving to an LLM is not. Even if you are writing in Javascript, you are still modelling a problem on to some representation in code. The only thing that is abstracted from you is memory management, a technical detail.

With an LLM you don't model the problem at all, you let something else do it. Moving from an low-code app builder to an LLM is a higher level of abstraction. Moving from writing code yourself to having an LLM write it is something different entirely.

(Though the author seems to be advocating against that style of usage, which I agree with.)

— anothaway · 20261125T21:58:20

↳ Reply to anothaway

> With an LLM you don't model the problem at all, you let something else do it.

I've been using Claude Code for many months now, and this is not my experience at all.

Whenever I work on something, I have a back-and-forth with Claude that make take anywhere from 3 to 30 turns to fully work out the model together, so that we both understand it completely. That's the hard part.

Then once it's all modeled, I have it write it all up as documentation, which I then read to review and correct anything wrong. In a 10-page document, there's usually a few sentences that need a slight clarification.

Then I start a fresh session, point it at the spec, and let Claude chug away at building it in code for 15 or 30 minutes. That's the easy part.

I feel like I'm still doing all the hard work of modeling everything that is important at the product/user level. But now I just get to skip the slog of coding itself.

To me, it very much does feel like moving up to a higher level of abstraction, where we're writing technical documentation in English together instead of technical code itself.

— crazygringo · 20261126T06:31:21

One thing I hate about the "it's just another higher-level abstraction" is the indeterminism. I don't understand or think it's reasonable to understand lower levels of abstraction given their complexity (but I have occasionally dug into niche cases when it's bit me and appreciate the ability to do so) but... We're shifting from a place where we use compilers to hide complexity to read and write at a rather concise portion of the stack to LLMs that allow us to write concisely but make us read pages of crap we shouldn't need to inspect.

If we had an LLM-like deterministic tool where our codebases just turned into the prompts (with the tuning to make everything right) and software dev turned into maintaining and designing those prompts I think we'd be in a much better place than we are now where we're making simple statements that should turn into complex machine code certainly - but first end up being saved for recall as partially interpreted verbosity... You explained what a price cartel is. In a healthy economy for consumers, companies are supposed to compete against each others and adapt to the demand. Increasing the supply does require a high CapEX, but they're expected to ramp up production of a product that can compete with rival companies' offerings. I'm not denying that "not taking risks and keeping the supply low" is better for them financially, it's a very reasonable choice to make more money. I'm saying that's the moment when it's reasonable to accuse them of anti-competitive practices. Companies must take risks and attempt to beat the competition.

There are a few:

- A massive expansion in userbase for what previously would have been considered high-performance computing equipment. Now that no particular skills whatsoever are required to harness these to some productive end, demand is presumably seeing a step-change up.

- Concentration/consolidation in manufacturing, largely unchecked by the partial lack of national, and complete lack of international guardrails against collusion (price fixing, supply limiting, etc)

I've been thinking and considering this a bit along with some some larger ideas. First, coming to terms would help:

"An abstraction is a simplified description, or specification, of a system that emphasizes some of the system's details or properties while suppressing others. A good abstraction is one in which information that is significant to the reader (i.e., the user) is emphasized while details that are immaterial or diversionary, at least for the moment, are suppressed... The abstractions we use for software tend to emphasize functional properties of the software, emphasizing what results are to be obtained and suppressing details about how this is to be achieved." -- Mary Shaw, Proceedings of the IEEE, Vol. 68, No. 9, 1980, pp. 1119–1130[0]

There are other definitions. But, with current paradigms being turned on their head a little, it's interesting to consider this instead of some that came later. Mary also notes: "As languages evolve to meet these ideas, we reshape our perceptions of the problems and solutions in response to the new experiences," so maybe we shouldn't be too locked into one way of thinking about this. I don't want to totally dismiss things like specifications, and she doesn't either, but it may just be a separate closely linked matter.

My current line of reasoning is that LLMs may be doing at least two things:

- 1) They offer a new sort of probabilistic or automated layer of abstraction, dynamically suppressing complexity. User's who only create software through natural language in the LLM are only reasoning about the functional properties they care about at that moment. In this sense, assuming the LLM can pull it off, maybe this is actually a fantastic abstraction. (That said, for now LLMs may struggle with aspects of execution in the same way "Programming By Example" did. Train of thought: In some sense, maybe prompting is a lossy specification.)

- 2) They allow users to move between or operate at multiple levels of abstraction. It's possible to define a model, to provide a spec, or to give the system a file with your own code and have it use those things. Sometimes you can do multiple at once. (Again, ignoring issues or reliability for the moment.)

People seem to find value in those tools. Some users are only able to leverage the first dynamic abstraction tool, but more knowledgeable users can also leverage the second.

So, I agree with the article author for the moment. This is a rapidly evolving toolkit that could be legitimacy useful and allow adding extra verification that wasn't economical before. Although LLMs are potentially making people stupid and building bad software, the bigger issue at the moment seems to be a an actual backlog of issues suddenly coming due.

Humans aren't perfect and software isn't perfect. There's always a need for trade-offs. Previously companies were able to aggressively trade-off toward profit motive and get away with it. Now the are cultural and structural issues are being exploited as the trade-offs change.

One thing that remains to be seen is if these new tools will actually allow validation and defense to stay ahead of attackers. It is possible that a few years from now, they aren't enough to protect against enhanced attacks. I wonder what the knock-on effect will be for things like insurance, but I'm not sure it's useful to dwell on it when things are evolving this rapidly.

💬 This is really cool. I have a suggestion, though: the samples within a button seem to have several modification types including a pitch shifter. For example, "DOWN4" under the "Multi-sampled sounds" heading sounds nearly a semitone lower than the other DOWN variants. I suggest eliminating all pitch shifting (or at least confining your use to a few cents), leaving only timbre variation. Go nuts creating variation through EQ, distortion, formant shifting, reflections/delay/reverb, etc. but keep the pitch locked. Why? Because the pitch of everything in this world is based on its resonant frequency, which is based on the size of whatever can vibrate, and in the case of a button it's resonating based on the size of the button. Many aspects of the sound would change based on things like how quickly the button is pushed or how much dampening the finger pushing it imparts, but the fundamental pitch is not one of them.

When playing a violin, if you move up the fingerboard, the pitch of the string increases. But if instead of playing the string you knock on the body as if knocking on someone's front door, the main pitch of that knocking never changes. The sympathetic vibrations of the strings will have frequencies that vary as the finger position varies, and the brightness and RT60 of the reverberation through the wood will vary from knock to knock, but the fundamental frequency generally excited by the knock only changes if the violin's volumetric size changes, and it never will.

Maybe a drum is a better example than a violin, since it's "unpitched" and yet still gets tuned to have some fundamental frequency. Only the noisy stuff varies from hit to hit, and the fundamental frequency does not (until you re-tune, or from temperature/humidity changing).

item.content:encoded:

Top Comments

💬 This is the single most important attack vector for SAAS companies. It has been for a long time --- this is the standard fact pattern for every SAAS breach --- but much more so today. As the number of employees grow, the likelihood that one of their laptops will get compromised approaches 1. When that happens, the attacker will be able to push code to Github, and if that code gets deployed, you're owned.

In 1Password's case, the absolute worst-case catastrophe is mitigated by the fact that customers retain custody of their unlocking secrets; 1Password (at least in the normal product flows) simply doesn't hold it. But an attack like this implicates every catastrophe short of that worst case.

Change velocity in 2026 is unreal and that trend is going to continue. You could not outcompete 1Password by building a handcrafted artisanal password manager backend (witness all the commercially successful password managers that don't even share 1Password's customer secret custody model). You have to accept insane PR rates as a premise to do modern SAAS security.

So the question then becomes: what is review? It's not what r/programming assumes it is; you almost certainly can't literally have a team of people line-by-line reviewing PRs anymore, at least not across the whole codebase (you can and should probably do a threat model for your codebase and institute stuff like that on a case-by-case basis, though). What you can realistically expect to review for is change provenance; a human developer signoff of some sort. But it's tricky! The attacker owns your email during the window of attack.

I think this is a fun problem to noodle on, and someone could probably come up with something here that would make a real difference.
